cases.expected: The draft belongs to A and is absent from B's listing.
cases.oracle: `company_id` on the created event group equals A. Also verify in the database (see API-DB-002).

cases.title: A draft with valid line items is created
cases.why: The base case; every flow in this file starts here.
cases.steps: `POST /api/event_groups` with `status: "draft"`, a title, and one line item (`product_id`, `quantity: {value, unit}`).
cases.expected: 200, an event group with one line-item id, status draft.
cases.oracle: `event_group_line_item_ids.length == 1`; `status == "draft"`.

cases.title: A missing status is refused
cases.why: `status` drives every downstream branch, so it is required rather than defaulted.
cases.steps: Omit `status`.
cases.expected: 422, code 2 "Insufficient parameters".
cases.oracle: No event group created.

cases.title: Blank line items are refused on a non-BOQ create
cases.why: An event with nothing to bid on is meaningless, and the rule is conditional on the BOQ flag — which makes it worth two cases.
cases.steps: `POST` with `line_items: []` and no `config.boq_based_rfx`.
cases.expected: 422, code 2.
cases.oracle: No event group created.

cases.title: A BOQ-based create succeeds with empty line items
cases.why: The one legal empty-items create, and the flag is what makes it legal.
cases.setup: A workspace with BOQ-in-eRFX allowed.
cases.steps: `POST` with `config.boq_based_rfx: true` and `line_items: []`.
cases.expected: 200, event group created with no line items.
cases.oracle: Created; zero line-item ids.

cases.title: A BOQ-based create is refused where the workspace forbids it
cases.why: Without the negative half, the gate is unproven — and a leak here lets an event exist with no items on a tenant that cannot handle it.
cases.setup: A workspace without BOQ-in-eRFX.
cases.steps: Same body as API-EG-004.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: A dormant-locked PR line item blocks the create before any write
cases.why: It has its own error shape (a dedicated dormant-PR renderer, not `render_error_json`), and the guard runs before the transaction — so a partial event must be impossible.
cases.setup: A PR line item under a dormant lock.
cases.steps: `POST` referencing it via `line_items[].pr_line_item_id`.
cases.expected: A dormant-PR error response.
cases.oracle: No event group **and** no line items in the database.

cases.title: A caller without trade create-record permission is refused
cases.why: The one authorization gate on this endpoint, and it is team-based.
cases.setup: A user whose teams lack `trade: create_record`.
cases.steps: `POST /api/event_groups`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: Title, description and attachments pass through unchanged
cases.why: They are stored verbatim; a transform here would be invisible until a vendor read it.
cases.steps: `POST` with all three set. Read the event group back.
cases.expected: Identical values.
cases.oracle: Field-by-field equality on the read.

cases.title: Two line items get serial numbers 1 and 2
cases.why: Serial numbers order the sheet and the award; duplicates or gaps scramble both.
cases.steps: `POST` with two line items.
cases.expected: Serials 1 and 2, in the order sent.
cases.oracle: Serial values and their order.

cases.title: The create response never contains a stage
cases.why: It is the structural fact the whole flow depends on. If a stage ever appeared here, the two-call model would have changed and every flow would need rewriting.
cases.steps: `POST` and inspect the response.
cases.expected: No `trade_request` / stage in the payload.
cases.oracle: No stage key present; `stages` empty or absent.

cases.title: A model validation failure surfaces the model's own message
cases.why: Code 15 "Operation failed" alone is useless; the endpoint overrides the message with the model's first error for a reason.
cases.setup: A payload that saves but fails `valid?`.
cases.steps: `POST`.
cases.expected: 422 code 15 whose message is the model's error text.
cases.oracle: Message is not the literal "Operation failed".

cases.title: Malformed line items are refused, not coerced
cases.why: PRD §5's "never a 500, never a silent partial save".
cases.steps: `POST` with `line_items` as a string, then as an object, then as an array of strings.
cases.expected: 4xx each time, with a readable message.
cases.oracle: No 500; nothing created.

cases.title: A line item with a non-existent product is refused
cases.why: A dangling product id produces an event nobody can bid on.
cases.steps: `POST` with a product id that does not exist.
cases.expected: Refused with a product error.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: A line item with a product from another company is refused
cases.why: It is a cross-tenant read dressed up as a create.
cases.steps: `POST` with company B's product id from company A's session.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing created; no cross-company row.

cases.title: A zero or negative quantity is refused
cases.why: PRD §5, at the layer that actually persists it.
cases.steps: `POST` with `quantity.value` of `0`, then `-5`.
cases.expected: Refused both times.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: A non-numeric quantity is refused rather than coerced
cases.why: A coerced `"abc" → 0` line item is a silently broken event.
cases.steps: `POST` with `quantity.value: "abc"`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No line item with quantity 0. ≈ BE-3.8's create-side twin.

cases.title: A missing quantity unit is refused
cases.why: Without a unit, a quantity cannot be compared against a bid, and the bid-side check (512) assumes the event has one.
cases.steps: `POST` with `quantity: {value: 10}`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: 65 line items are accepted on a non-BOQ create
cases.why: The documented cap, at the API layer where the UI's message does not exist.
cases.steps: `POST` with 65 line items.
cases.expected: 200 with 65 line-item ids.
cases.oracle: Count is exactly 65.

cases.title: 501 BOQ line items are refused
cases.why: The other cap, and the case that shows whether the limit is enforced server-side or only in the browser.
cases.setup: A BOQ-allowed workspace.
cases.steps: `POST` with 501 line items.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing created — a UI-only limit would show as a 200 here, which is the finding.

cases.title: A created event group is assigned a reference id
cases.why: `add_ref_id` runs `after_create_commit` via `update_columns`, bypassing validations and callbacks — a path where a failure is easy to miss.
cases.steps: `POST`, then read the event group back.
cases.expected: A `RFX-…` reference id.
cases.oracle: Ref id present and unique. Confirm in the database (API-DB-003).

cases.title: An RFQ stage is created against a draft event group
cases.why: The most common stage, and the one every bid case needs.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/template_input` with `rfx_mode: rfq`, `event_group_id`, `trade_products`, `bid_start_time`, `bid_end_time`, `status: "draft"`.
cases.expected: 200 with a trade uuid linked to the event group.
cases.oracle: The trade's `event_group_id` matches; `rfx_mode` is rfq.

cases.title: An auction stage is created with a rank strategy
cases.why: The default auction shape, and the strategy travels in nested `configurations` rather than at the top level — easy to send in the wrong place.
cases.steps: `POST` with `rfx_mode: auction` and a rank auction config.
cases.expected: Created with `auction_config` rank.
cases.oracle: Strategy on the created trade is rank.

cases.title: An auction stage is created with a price strategy
cases.why: The second strategy, to prove the config is read rather than defaulted.
cases.steps: As above with a price config.
cases.expected: Created with price.
cases.oracle: Strategy is price, not rank.

cases.title: A technical (RFP) stage is created without trade products
cases.why: `trade_products` is required *unless* the stage is RFI/RFP. The exemption is the case worth proving; sending products anyway is how RFP stages end up looking like pricing stages.
cases.steps: `POST` with `rfx_mode: rfp`, a technical template and an evaluator, no `trade_products`.
cases.expected: Created.
cases.oracle: Stage created with rfx_mode rfp and no trade products.

cases.title: A pricing stage without trade products is refused
cases.why: The other side of the same rule ("Product not found", 80).
cases.steps: `POST` with `rfx_mode: rfq` and no `trade_products`.
cases.oracle: No stage created.

cases.title: An RFI stage is created
cases.why: `rfi` is in the enum but not in `STANDARD_STAGES_SEQUENCE` and has no UI on this build, so the API is the only way to prove it works — or that it does not.
cases.steps: `POST` with `rfx_mode: rfi`.
cases.expected: Created; it uses generic `bidding_time` schedules rather than rfq/auction ones.
cases.oracle: Stage created; its schedule type is `bidding_time`.

cases.title: An offline-trade stage is created where the tenant allows it
cases.why: It is a legitimate event type with no bidding window semantics, and it is also excluded from stage ordering.
cases.setup: gate: offline trade enabled.
cases.steps: `POST` with `rfx_mode: offline_trade`.
cases.expected: Created.
cases.oracle: Stage created; surrogate/bid behaviour differs (see API-SUR-003).

cases.title: A stage in a `sell`-mode workspace is refused
cases.why: The first guard on this endpoint, and it fails before anything else is validated.
cases.setup: A workspace with `trade_mode == "sell"`.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/template_input`.
cases.oracle: No stage created.

cases.title: A product not allowed for the workspace is refused
cases.why: Allowed-products validation runs before existence checks, so its own error code matters.
cases.steps: `POST` with a product outside the allowed set.
cases.expected: Refused with the specific allowed-products error.
cases.oracle: No stage created; the code is not the generic 80.

cases.title: A non-existent product is refused with "Product not found"
cases.why: The existence check, distinct from the allowed check.
cases.steps: `POST` with a fabricated product id.
cases.oracle: No stage created.

cases.title: Too many attachments on a stage are refused
cases.why: Code 489 with a readable message, and it is a cheap DoS vector if unbounded.
cases.steps: `POST` with attachments beyond the limit.
cases.oracle: No stage created.

cases.title: Knockout combined with a basket auction is refused
cases.why: An explicitly forbidden configuration (474), and forbidden combinations are exactly what an API-level suite should hold.
cases.steps: `POST` with a knockout auction config and basket auction on.
cases.oracle: No stage created.

cases.title: A dutch auction combined with a basket auction is refused
cases.why: Same guard, other strategy.
cases.steps: `POST` with dutch + basket.
cases.oracle: No stage created.

cases.title: A stage always gets a bidding-time schedule row
cases.why: This row is the one the activation path dereferences unguarded. Its existence at creation is the single most load-bearing fact in this file.
cases.steps: `POST` with `bid_start_time` and `bid_end_time` as epoch seconds. Read the stage's schedules.
cases.expected: A `TradeSchedule` in the bidding-time family with both times set.
cases.oracle: Verify in the database, not only in the response — the response can echo times the row does not have. Pairs with API-PUB-002.

cases.title: A stage created with no bid_end_time fails at creation, not later
cases.why: `trade_schedules.end_time` is `NOT NULL` in the database, so this either fails here with a constraint error or — worse — creates a stage with no schedule that explodes at activation.
cases.steps: `POST` omitting `bid_end_time`.
cases.expected: Refused at creation with a readable error.
cases.oracle: No stage created **and** no schedule row. A 200 here is the finding: it means the failure has been deferred to activation.

cases.title: An end time before the start time is refused
cases.why: `TradeSchedule` has **no Rails validations at all**, so chronology is only enforced by callers. That makes this a genuine hole worth probing.
cases.steps: `POST` with `bid_end_time < bid_start_time`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No stage created. If it is accepted, record the inverted window as a finding and check what the vendor's portal does with it.

cases.title: An eRFX stage does not take its audience at creation
cases.why: `audience_company_ids` is applied here only when `event_group_id` is nil. An eRFX stage gets its audience at activation instead — so a test that invites vendors here and then asserts they are on the stage is asserting the wrong step.
cases.steps: `POST` with both `event_group_id` and `audience_company_ids`.
cases.expected: Created; no audience rows yet.
cases.oracle: Audience count on the stage is 0 before activation.

cases.title: A non-eRFX stage does take its audience at creation
cases.why: The other branch, and it is how the classic single-stage events in UI §14 get their participants.
cases.steps: `POST` with `audience_company_ids` and no `event_group_id`.
cases.expected: Created with the audience applied.
cases.oracle: Audience count matches the request.

cases.title: A non-eRFX stage created with status active goes live directly
cases.why: The baseline contrast case: this path worked throughout the eRFX activation regression, which is what proved the fault was specific to the event-group update.
cases.steps: `POST` with `status: "active"`, no event group.
cases.expected: 200; the stage is live and biddable.
cases.oracle: Stage status active; a vendor bid on it is accepted.

cases.title: A knockout or dutch stage created active publishes inline
cases.why: Those two modes call `publish_auction` immediately at creation; **every other mode does not**. That asymmetry is a prime suspect for activation-path bugs and needs to be pinned.
cases.steps: `POST` a knockout auction with `status: "active"`.
cases.expected: Created and published in the same call.
cases.oracle: The auction's schedule and state reflect a published auction. Contrast with API-STG-021.

cases.title: A plain auction created active does not publish inline
cases.why: It documents the asymmetry rather than assuming symmetry — and it is the difference that makes the activation path load-bearing at all.
cases.steps: `POST` a rank auction with `status: "active"`.
cases.expected: Created without `publish_auction` having run.
cases.oracle: Compare the resulting state against API-STG-020's; record the difference.

cases.title: A draft stage links to an existing draft event group
cases.why: It is the link that makes the two-call model work; a broken link produces an event group with no stages and an orphan trade.
cases.steps: `POST` with `event_group_id` of an existing draft.
cases.expected: Created and linked.
cases.oracle: The event group's stage list contains it. ≈ BE-10.4.

cases.title: Updating a draft stage via template_input strips the status
cases.why: `template_input_trade_update` deliberately removes `status` so the update runs the draft-save path rather than draft→active. Without that, editing a scheduled draft would publish it.
cases.setup: A draft stage on a scheduled template.
cases.steps: `PATCH /trade/:id/template_input` with `status: "active"`.
cases.expected: The stage stays draft; the other edits apply.
cases.oracle: Status still draft after the call.

cases.title: Adding a stage to a live event uses its own endpoint and policy
cases.why: The policy allows either the event's owner or anyone with create access — a wider gate than stage creation, and worth confirming rather than assuming.
cases.setup: A live event; a non-owner buyer with create access.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/:id/add_new_stage_in_live_event` as each.
cases.expected: Both allowed; a user with neither is refused.
cases.oracle: Three outcomes as expected; the live event's existing stage is untouched.

cases.title: A fresh single-stage draft activates
cases.why: The happy-path baseline the rest of the section is measured against.
cases.setup: A draft event group with one draft stage that has a bidding-time schedule.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "active"` and the stage uuid in `draft_trade_request_uuids`.
cases.expected: 200; the event group is active with one live stage.
cases.oracle: Status active; the stage appears in `stages`; a vendor can bid on it.

cases.title: Activation must never answer with an untyped 500
cases.why: The standing regression. From ~16:29 on 2026-09-08 this endpoint returned `{"status":500,"error":"Internal Server Error"}` for **both** `status: "active"` and `status: "draft"`, invariant across stage type (auction / RFQ / RFP), line-item count (1 or 2), invited vendors (0, 1, 154), sheet filled or empty, and schedule default or explicitly saved. Nothing was written — the title never appeared in the events list — so the raise happened before the commit.
cases.setup: Any valid draft event group and stage.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate. Capture the full response body and the request payload.
cases.expected: Either 200, or a `render_error_json` failure with a `{code, message}`.
cases.oracle: Fail if the body is `{"status":500,"error":…}` with no code. Attach the payload to the failure — the payload is what makes the report actionable. The three ranked causes are a `lock_transaction` double-render at `event_groups_controller.rb:74`, `set_customized_audiences` (`trade_controller_helper.rb:687-729`), and `TradeSchedule.change_auction_time(nil)` in `publish_auction`; the third cannot explain the draft-status 500, so an exception class from Sentry is what distinguishes them.

cases.title: Activation of a stage with no bidding-time schedule fails cleanly
cases.why: `change_auction_time(nil)` has no nil guard, so this is a real unguarded dereference. The correct behaviour is a refusal naming the schedule.
cases.setup: A draft stage whose bidding-time `TradeSchedule` is absent.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate.
cases.expected: A `{code, message}` refusal about the schedule.
cases.oracle: Not a bare 500. This is the regression guard's narrowest form.

cases.title: Activation succeeds identically for auction, rfq and rfp stages
cases.why: Publishing must not be strategy-sensitive; if one mode fails, the cause is in that mode's setup rather than in publish.
cases.steps: Build three single-stage drafts, one per mode. Activate each.
cases.expected: All three activate.
cases.oracle: Three active events; report per-mode outcomes separately so a single failure is attributable.

cases.title: Activation succeeds with one line item and with several
cases.why: It rules line-item count in or out as a factor — which is exactly what the regression investigation needed.
cases.steps: Activate a 1-item event and a 2-item event.
cases.expected: Both succeed.
cases.oracle: Both active with the expected item counts.

cases.title: Activation succeeds with a single invited vendor
cases.why: The minimum useful audience, and the fixture every bid case needs.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with one `audience_company_uuids` entry.
cases.expected: Active with that vendor invited.
cases.oracle: One audience row for the stage; the vendor can see the event.

cases.title: Activation succeeds with a large audience below the cap
cases.why: Large audiences are normal on real tenants (154 on one client), and they are where the audience-application code path gets exercised properly.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with ~150 vendor uuids.
cases.expected: Active with all of them invited.
cases.oracle: Audience count equals the request; record the duration.

cases.title: More than 500 new audience companies is refused
cases.why: The explicit cap ("Participants limit exceeded. Maximum 500 participants are allowed.", 511), enforced during publish.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with 501 uuids.
cases.oracle: The event is not activated with 501; the message names the limit.

cases.title: Activation succeeds with the pricing sheet filled and with it empty
cases.why: It separates sheet completeness from activation. The UI enforces "sheet partially filled"; the API's tolerance is the thing to know.
cases.steps: Activate with sheet values present, then with none.
cases.expected: Both succeed at the API layer, or the refusal is a readable one.
cases.oracle: Record both outcomes; a 500 on either is the finding.

cases.title: Activating a non-existent event group is refused
cases.why: The first precondition, and it must not be a 500.
cases.steps: `PATCH /api/event_groups/<fabricated>`.
cases.expected: 422, code 533 "Project does not exist."
cases.oracle: That code and message.

cases.title: Activating a superseded version is refused
cases.why: `latest?` is checked before any write; without it, a stale client could overwrite newer work.
cases.setup: An event group with a newer version.
cases.steps: `PATCH` the older one.
cases.oracle: The newer version is untouched.

cases.title: An attachment URL from another company is refused
cases.why: Every attachment URL is validated for company ownership before anything else happens; it is a cross-tenant read vector.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with an attachment URL owned by another company.
cases.oracle: Nothing written; the event stays draft.

cases.title: A caller without update permission is refused
cases.why: The policy has two independent branches (Procol employee acting as CSM, or allowed-company plus trade create) and both need proving.
cases.setup: A user in neither branch.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Event unchanged.

cases.title: A Procol-employee CSM can update without the trade permission flag
cases.why: The other policy branch. It is a deliberate back door for support, and it must work for the right people and nobody else.
cases.setup: A Procol employee who is CSM for the company, without `trade: create_record`.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to update.
cases.expected: Allowed.
cases.oracle: The update applies. Then repeat as a Procol employee who is *not* CSM for that company — that must be refused.

cases.title: Publishing RFP + RFQ where the RFP ends later is refused
cases.why: Code 712, "RFP duration exceeds RFQ end time. Please adjust." — a real ordering constraint between stage windows.
cases.setup: A two-stage draft with the RFP ending after the RFQ.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate both.
cases.oracle: Neither stage goes live.

cases.title: A `purchase_request_id` must resolve to an active BOQ PR in the workspace
cases.why: An unvalidated link would attach an event to a foreign or inactive requisition.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with an inactive PR id, then with another workspace's PR id.
cases.expected: Refused both times (101).
cases.oracle: No link created.

cases.title: A draft-status PATCH with line items takes the generic branch
cases.why: It is the autosave path, and confusing it with publish is how a draft accidentally goes live.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "draft"` and `line_items` present.
cases.expected: Line items are updated; the event stays draft.
cases.oracle: Status draft; line items reflect the payload.

cases.title: Line items sent with `status: "active"` are ignored
cases.why: They are only read on the generic branch. Silently ignoring them is the documented behaviour, and a test expecting otherwise chases a phantom.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate with a new line item in `line_items`.
cases.expected: Activation succeeds; the new line item is **not** created.
cases.oracle: Line-item count unchanged. Record it as expected behaviour, not a bug — but flag it if the UI ever relies on it.

cases.title: `status: "active"` on an already-active event with no draft stages runs no service
cases.why: Neither branch guard matches, so no service is called and the controller still renders with variables that were never assigned. That is a latent edge case, and this is the case that watches it.
cases.setup: An active event group, no `draft_trade_request_ids`, no `line_items`, no `config`.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "active"`.
cases.expected: A coherent response — not a 500, not a silent state change.
cases.oracle: Assert no state change **and** no 500. ≈ BE-9.6.

cases.title: Re-activating an already-active event is idempotent
cases.why: Clients retry. A retry that duplicates stages or audiences is a data-integrity bug.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate twice with identical bodies.
cases.expected: No duplicates.
cases.oracle: Stage count, audience count and bid count identical after the second call.

cases.title: Transient config keys are stripped from the persisted config
cases.why: `is_scheduled_template`, `schedule`, `ends_at` and `max_occurrences` are deliberately removed; a leak would make an ordinary event behave like a recurring template.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with all four in `config`. Read the event group back.
cases.expected: None of them are persisted.
cases.oracle: All four absent from the stored config.

cases.title: A terms attachment missing its `type` key is refused cleanly
cases.why: The structure is rehydrated into a PORO, so a missing key is a prime candidate for an unhandled exception — precisely what PRD §5 forbids.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `terms_and_conditions.attachments: [{value: []}]`.
cases.expected: A 4xx with a readable message.

cases.title: Absent `terms_and_conditions.clauses` does not crash activation
cases.why: The UI sends an empty-but-present structure; other clients may send neither. Both must work.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with clauses nil, then with the whole key absent.
cases.expected: Activation succeeds both ways.
cases.oracle: No 500; the stored terms are empty rather than null-broken. ≈ BE-2.24.

cases.title: A stage absent from `draft_trade_request_uuids` is voided
cases.why: Any stage on the event group not named in the publish gets voided. A ghost stage that survived would accept bids nobody expects.
cases.setup: A draft event group with three draft stages.
cases.steps: `PATCH` naming two of them.
cases.expected: Two live stages; the third voided.
cases.oracle: The third stage's status is `void`; it is absent from the read payload. ≈ BE-9.3.

cases.title: Adding a draft stage to an already-live event publishes just that stage
cases.why: It is the second publish-branch trigger, and it must not re-publish or disturb the live stage.
cases.setup: A live event plus a new draft stage on the same event group.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "active"` and only the new stage's uuid.
cases.expected: The new stage goes live; the existing one is untouched, bids intact.
cases.oracle: Stage count +1; the original stage's bid count unchanged. ≈ BE-2.19.

cases.title: Activating an event group with zero stages is a safe no-op
cases.why: The publish loop over stages must tolerate an empty set rather than raising on it.
cases.setup: A draft event group with no stages.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate.
cases.expected: A coherent response, no exception.
cases.oracle: No 500; the resulting state is explainable. ≈ BE-9.5.

cases.title: An approval-gated stage becomes `requested`, not `active`
cases.why: On those tenants "published" means "pending approval", so an assertion of active is wrong there and would look like a publish failure.
cases.setup: gate: publish approval configured.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate.
cases.expected: Stage status `requested`; an approval record exists.
cases.oracle: Status requested; approval present. ≈ BE-9.7.

cases.title: Auto-routing to the auction team forces the stage to `draft`
cases.why: gate: `routeAuctionsToAuctionTeam`. It looks exactly like a failed publish unless you know.
cases.setup: gate: `routeAuctionsToAuctionTeam`. An auction stage.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate.
cases.expected: Stage status draft, assigned to the auction team.
cases.oracle: Status draft plus the assignment. ≈ BE-9.8.

cases.title: Activation fires invitation mails exactly once
cases.why: Three `after_commit` callbacks fire on the draft→active transition, each guarded against scheduled templates and dummy event groups. Two invitation mails per vendor is a support call; zero is a dead event.
cases.steps: Activate, then re-issue the same activation.
cases.expected: One invitation per vendor overall.
cases.oracle: Count the enqueued mail jobs across both calls.

cases.title: The activation response carries the full published shape
cases.why: The response is what the UI renders straight after publish; a missing key there is what makes the screen look broken after a successful publish.
cases.steps: Activate and inspect the response.
cases.expected: `stages`, `stage_vs_participants_data`, `config` (including `should_allow_awarding`) and `is_bid_placed_globally` all present.
cases.oracle: Each key present and internally consistent with the request.

cases.title: A line item is added to a draft via the generic branch
cases.why: The only way to add an item after creation.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "draft"` and an extra entry in `line_items`.
cases.expected: The item is created and returned in the new ids.
cases.oracle: Line-item count +1. ≈ BE-3.1.

cases.title: Deleting a line item on a draft sets it inactive
cases.why: Drafts soft-delete to `in_active`, active events to `deleted` — two different terminal states, and confusing them makes a read filter wrong.
cases.steps: Delete a line item on a draft.
cases.expected: Status `in_active`.
cases.oracle: The row's status is exactly `in_active`. ≈ BE-3.4.

cases.title: Deleting a line item on an active event sets it deleted and voids associations
cases.why: The associated `TradeProduct`, `Form` and mapping rows must go with it, or the sheet keeps rendering a phantom row.
cases.steps: Delete a line item on an active event.
cases.expected: Status `deleted`; associations void/inactive; PR quantity reconciled.
cases.oracle: Verify each association's status in the database. ≈ BE-3.3.

cases.title: Deleting the only line item is refused
cases.why: Code 711 — it would leave an event with nothing to bid on.
cases.steps: Delete the sole line item.
cases.oracle: The item remains active. ≈ BE-3.10.

cases.title: Deleting the last remaining *active* line item is refused
cases.why: Distinct from API-LI-004: several rows may exist with only one active. The rule is about the active count.
cases.setup: Three line items, two already deleted.
cases.steps: Delete the third.
cases.oracle: The active count stays 1.

cases.title: Deleting a line item referenced by a valid proposal is refused
cases.why: It would orphan an award in progress.
cases.setup: A requested or selected proposal referencing the item.
cases.steps: Delete it.
cases.oracle: The proposal is intact. ≈ BE-3.2.

cases.title: Replacing BOQ line items deletes the old set and creates the new
cases.why: Appending instead of replacing silently doubles a 500-row event.
cases.steps: Send a new set of BOQ line items on a generic-branch update.
cases.expected: The old ones are deleted, the new ones created.
cases.oracle: Active count equals the new set's size, not the sum. ≈ BE-3.7.

cases.title: A string quantity is refused, not coerced
cases.why: PRD §5. A coerced `0` quantity is an event nobody can price.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `quantity.value: "ten"`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No line item with quantity 0. ≈ BE-3.8.

cases.title: Line-item deletion enqueues its cleanup worker
cases.why: The `after_update_commit` callbacks are what actually clean up; a deletion that skips them leaves stale derived data.
cases.steps: Delete a line item.
cases.expected: The deletion and event-group update workers are enqueued.
cases.oracle: Both jobs present. ≈ BE-3.9.

cases.title: Updating a line item's quantity reconciles the PR
cases.why: The requisition's in-progress quantity is derived from this; drift here means the PR never closes correctly.
cases.setup: A PR-linked event.
cases.steps: Reduce a line item's quantity.
cases.expected: The PR's in-progress quantity matches.
cases.oracle: Read the PR and compare.

cases.title: `update_egli` is refused outside evaluation time
cases.why: Code 741 — evaluator changes mid-bidding would change the scoring after the fact.
cases.setup: A stage not in extra-closing/evaluation time.
cases.steps: `PATCH /event_groups/update_egli`.
cases.oracle: Evaluators unchanged. ≈ BE-3.5.

cases.title: `update_egli` without a form id is refused
cases.why: The lookup is by `form_id`; a missing one must be a 422, not a nil dereference.
cases.steps: `PATCH /event_groups/update_egli` with no `form_id`.
cases.expected: 422, code 2.
cases.oracle: That code; no 500. ≈ BE-3.6.

cases.title: `update_egli` succeeds inside evaluation time
cases.why: The positive half; without it API-LI-011 could pass on a broken endpoint.
cases.setup: A stage in evaluation time.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with a valid form id and evaluators.
cases.expected: 200; evaluators updated.
cases.oracle: The new evaluators are on the line item.

cases.title: Line items are readable back with their quantities and products
cases.why: PRD §3.6 — every created event must be retrievable. This is the read half.
cases.steps: `GET /event_groups/:uuid/get_line_items`.
cases.expected: Every active item with its product, quantity and unit.
cases.oracle: Count and values match what was created.

cases.title: Activation applies the audience per stage
cases.why: For eRFX, this is the only point at which vendors are invited — the stage-creation call ignores the audience (API-STG-017).
cases.steps: Activate with `audience_company_uuids`. Read the audience.
cases.expected: One active row per company per stage.
cases.oracle: `GET /event_groups/:uuid/get_audience` returns exactly those companies.

cases.title: The invited vendor can read the event
cases.why: The invitation is only real if it grants read access; the policy needs both trade-read *and* a visible stage.
cases.steps: As the invited vendor, `GET /api/event_groups/:id`.
cases.expected: 200 with the event.
cases.oracle: The response contains the event's line items and its own stage.

cases.title: A vendor with no visible stage cannot read the event
cases.why: `show?` requires `get_valid_stages_for_user` to be non-empty, so a vendor with read permission and no stage is refused. It is a rule people forget.
cases.setup: A vendor on the platform, not on any stage's audience.
cases.steps: `GET /api/event_groups/:id`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No event payload. ≈ BE-8.1.

cases.title: 501 new audience companies on one stage is refused
cases.why: The 500 cap, enforced at publish (511).
cases.steps: Activate with 501 uuids.
cases.oracle: Not activated with 501.

cases.title: One company cannot hold two active audience rows on one stage
cases.why: It is the model's own invariant, and violating it double-counts a vendor everywhere.
cases.steps: Apply the same company twice to one stage.
cases.expected: Still one active row.
cases.oracle: Count active rows in the database for that (company, stage). ≈ BE-4.7.

cases.title: Repeating the same activation does not duplicate audience rows
cases.why: The retry case for the same invariant, and the one a client actually causes.
cases.steps: Issue the identical activation `PATCH` twice.
cases.expected: No new rows.
cases.oracle: Active audience count identical. ≈ BE-9.4.

cases.title: Removing a vendor who has not participated succeeds
cases.why: The legal removal path, and the baseline for the refusal below.
cases.steps: Remove an invited vendor with no bid.
cases.expected: Their row becomes inactive/invisible; they can no longer read the event.
cases.oracle: As that vendor, the read is refused.

cases.title: Removing a vendor who already participated is refused
cases.why: Code 512-family guard — removing a bidder would silently invalidate a bid.
cases.setup: A vendor with a submitted bid.
cases.steps: Attempt the removal.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: The bid is still counted. ≈ BE-4.8.

cases.title: Hiding a vendor with an active bid is reported, not raised
cases.why: The callback emits a Sentry message rather than raising, so nothing visible happens — this case is the only way it is ever noticed.
cases.steps: Flip a bidding vendor's visibility to `no`.
cases.expected: The change is recorded; the bid remains reachable by the buyer.
cases.oracle: The buyer can still read the bid afterwards.

cases.title: Live-auction audience addition requires view access
cases.why: `add_audience_live_auction?` is gated only on view access — a wider gate than publish, which makes it worth confirming that it is at least that.
cases.setup: A user without view access to the event.
cases.steps: `PATCH /v1/trade/add_audience?id=…`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No audience row created. ≈ BE-4.9.

cases.title: A vendor self-participates on an active open-tender event
cases.why: The only path where a vendor joins uninvited, and it needs `open_tenders` on the company.
cases.setup: gate: `open_tenders`. An active event.
cases.steps: `POST /api/event_groups/:id/participants` as the vendor.
cases.expected: 200; an audience row with source self-registered.
cases.oracle: The buyer's participant list includes them, marked self-registered. ≈ BE-4.1.

cases.title: Self-participation on a non-active event is refused
cases.why: The lookup is scoped to active events, so a draft must answer 533 rather than joining.
cases.steps: `POST` participants on a draft event.
cases.oracle: No audience row. ≈ BE-4.2.

cases.title: Self-participation is refused without open tenders
cases.why: The gate. Without it, any vendor could join any active event.
cases.setup: A company without `open_tenders`.
cases.steps: `POST` participants.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No audience row. ≈ BE-4.3.

cases.title: Rejecting a participant requires remarks
cases.why: Code 752 — the remark is the audit trail for excluding a bidder.
cases.steps: `PATCH /api/event_groups/:id/reject_participant` with blank remarks.
cases.oracle: The participant is unchanged. ≈ BE-4.4.

cases.title: Rejecting a participant is refused for a caller who is neither purchaser nor auction team
cases.why: The check is inline in the action rather than in the policy, which is exactly the kind of check that disappears in a refactor.
cases.setup: A buyer who is neither.
cases.steps: `PATCH .../reject_participant` with valid remarks.
cases.expected: Refused (101).
cases.oracle: No rejection recorded. ≈ BE-4.6.

cases.title: A successful rejection is written by bypassing callbacks, and still consistent
cases.why: It appends to precomputed data with `update_columns` — no callbacks, no validations — and enqueues a worker. Anything derived from that field must still agree afterwards.
cases.steps: Reject a participant. Re-read the event.
cases.expected: The rejected company is listed as rejected everywhere it appears.
cases.oracle: The precomputed rejected list and the participant view agree.

cases.title: A vendor starts a technical response
cases.why: The first of the three calls; the uuid it returns keys the other two.
cases.setup: A live RFP stage with the vendor invited.
cases.steps: `POST /template_responses` for the technical trade.
cases.expected: 200 with a response uuid.
cases.oracle: Uuid returned and readable back.

cases.title: The technical trade exposes its forms and pages
cases.why: The answer payload is keyed by form and page uuids, which must be read from the trade rather than guessed. On this build the line-item form is the second entry, and the global one the first.
cases.steps: `GET /trade/:id` for the technical stage and read `sheets.forms`.
cases.expected: A global form and one line-item form, each with page uuids.
cases.oracle: Both forms present with non-empty page uuid lists — read the index from the payload rather than hard-coding it.

cases.title: Answers are saved to the line-item form
cases.why: The middle call; a wrong form uuid saves answers nobody reads.
cases.steps: `PUT /template_responses/:uuid/create_page_responses` with the line-item form and page.
cases.expected: 200; the answers are readable back on the response.
cases.oracle: Read the response and compare the answers.

cases.title: The response is submitted and visible to the buyer
cases.why: Submission is what makes it evaluable; a draft response is not a participation.
cases.steps: `PATCH /template_responses/:uuid` to submit.
cases.expected: Submitted state.
cases.oracle: The buyer's read of the event shows a submitted response for that vendor.

cases.title: An unanswered required question blocks submission
cases.why: An incomplete questionnaire cannot be scored fairly.
cases.steps: Submit with a required answer missing.
cases.expected: Refused, naming the gap.
cases.oracle: The response is not in a submitted state.

cases.title: A vendor cannot start a response on a stage they are not on
cases.why: It is a write path into another event's data.
cases.setup: A vendor not on the stage's audience.
cases.steps: `POST /template_responses` for that stage.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No response created.

cases.title: A vendor cannot read another vendor's response
cases.why: PRD §7.2 extends past prices — a competitor's technical answers are commercially sensitive too.
cases.setup: Two vendors with responses.
cases.steps: As A, `GET /template_responses/:B_uuid`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No payload for B.

cases.title: Submitting twice does not create a second response
cases.why: Idempotency on the vendor's most retried call.
cases.steps: Submit the same response twice.
cases.expected: One submitted response.
cases.oracle: Response count for that vendor is 1.

cases.title: A response cannot be started before the window opens
cases.why: Same fairness rule as bidding, on the technical stage.
cases.setup: An Upcoming RFP stage.
cases.steps: `POST /template_responses`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No response created.

cases.title: A response cannot be submitted after the window closes
cases.why: A late technical response changes the qualification set after the fact.
cases.setup: A closed RFP stage with a started response.
cases.steps: Submit.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: The response stays unsubmitted.

cases.title: An evaluator can score a submitted response
cases.why: It closes the RFP loop and feeds the awarding comparison.
cases.setup: gate: evaluation. A submitted response, stage in evaluation time.
cases.steps: `POST /evaluations`, then `POST /evaluations/submit`.
cases.expected: The score is saved and visible to the buyer.
cases.oracle: The buyer's read shows a non-empty evaluation score for that vendor.

cases.title: A non-evaluator cannot submit an evaluation
cases.why: Scores decide who qualifies; the wrong person scoring is an integrity failure.
cases.setup: A buyer who is not an assigned evaluator.
cases.steps: `POST /evaluations/submit`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No score recorded.

cases.title: An eligible vendor creates a bid
cases.why: The base case. Everything else in this section is a variation.
cases.setup: A live RFQ stage with the vendor invited.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids` with the trade and company.
cases.expected: 200 with a bid uuid.
cases.oracle: Uuid returned; the bid is readable back. ≈ BE-5.1.

cases.title: Bid products carry the price and quantity per line item
cases.why: The bid is a container; the prices live in the products. A bid with no products is a participation with no offer.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids/:uuid/create_bid_products` with one entry per line item.
cases.expected: 200; each line item has a price and quantity.
cases.oracle: Product count equals the line-item count; prices as sent.

cases.title: The bid is submitted and the total is what was offered
cases.why: The total is the number the buyer compares and the award is based on. A derivation error here is invisible and expensive.
cases.steps: `PATCH /v1/bids/:uuid` to submit, with the computed total.
cases.expected: 200; the bid is active with that total.
cases.oracle: Total equals the sum of price × quantity across the products, at the template's precision.

cases.title: A bid with no products is refused on submission
cases.why: The model validates it ("Please bid on at least one product") for non-fast, non-buyer-added bids.
cases.steps: Create a bid, skip the products, submit.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: The bid does not become active. `bid.rb:216-222`.

cases.title: A bid outside the window is refused
cases.why: Code 33 "Order not active" — the single most important fairness rule in the module.
cases.steps: Create a bid on a closed stage, then on an Upcoming one.
cases.expected: Refused both times.
cases.oracle: No bid created in either case.

cases.title: A bid on a withdrawn event is refused
cases.why: Withdrawal must be immediate at the API layer, not just in the UI.
cases.steps: Create a bid on a withdrawn event's stage.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid created.

cases.title: A vendor not on the audience is refused
cases.why: With an open policy layer, this is where invitation is actually enforced.
cases.setup: A vendor not invited.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid created — a 200 here would be a serious finding.

cases.title: A user cannot bid for a company they are not entitled to
cases.why: `can_place_bid_for_company` is what stops one vendor bidding as another.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids` with another company's uuid.
cases.expected: Refused (101).
cases.oracle: No bid created for that company.

cases.title: The buying company cannot bid on its own event
cases.why: Code 165, "Cannot place bid on trade by your own company".
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids` with the buyer's own company id, as a non-surrogate bid.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid created.

cases.title: A second bid from the same company is refused
cases.why: Code 99 / 96 — the check is at company and team level, which is the level that matters commercially.
cases.setup: A vendor with an active bid.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids` again.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: One active bid for that company.

cases.title: A bid from a subsidiary of an existing bidder is refused
cases.why: `is_part_of_subsidiary_network?` prevents one corporate group bidding twice under different names — a genuine collusion control.
cases.setup: Two companies in one subsidiary network; one has bid.
cases.steps: Bid as the other.
cases.expected: Refused (96).
cases.oracle: One bid across the network.

cases.title: Bidding after revoking is refused
cases.why: Code 370. Revocation is meant to be final within the event.
cases.setup: A vendor whose bid is revoked.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No new bid.

cases.title: Bidding is refused once the RFQ's auction exists
cases.why: Code 769, "You cannot edit rfq once the auction is created." It is the first guard in the sequence, so it also proves the ordering.
cases.setup: A converted RFQ.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids` on the RFQ.
cases.expected: Refused with 769.
cases.oracle: That specific code — not 33 — which is what confirms the guard order.

cases.title: Rebidding is refused where the seller is barred from it
cases.why: `not_allow_rebidding_to_seller?` is a per-event configuration and a silent bypass would let a barred vendor improve their price.
cases.setup: An event configured to bar rebidding.
cases.steps: Bid, then attempt a revision.
cases.expected: The revision is refused (101).
cases.oracle: The original bid is unchanged.

cases.title: A negative price is refused
cases.why: Code 106, checked on every product in the payload.
cases.steps: `POST` bid products with `price: -100`.
cases.oracle: No bid product created.

cases.title: A negative quantity is refused
cases.why: Code 35, a separate check from price.
cases.steps: `POST` bid products with a negative quantity.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: A negative GST is refused
cases.why: Code 107 — the third of the three per-product checks, and the one most likely to be forgotten.
cases.steps: `POST` bid products with a negative GST.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: A discount above 100 percent is refused
cases.why: Code 369 — above 100% inverts the price, which no downstream arithmetic expects.
cases.steps: `POST` with `trade_credit_discount.discount: 150`.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: A negative discount is refused
cases.why: Same check, other end of the range.
cases.steps: `POST` with a negative discount.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: Legacy top-level price and quantity fields are validated too
cases.why: The controller validates both the nested products *and* the older flat fields. An unvalidated legacy path is a real bypass for old clients.
cases.steps: `POST` with a top-level negative `price`, then a negative `quantity`, then a negative `gst`.
cases.expected: Refused each time (106 / 35 / 107).
cases.oracle: Nothing created in any case.

cases.title: A non-numeric price is refused, not coerced
cases.why: A coerced `0` is a winning bid.
cases.steps: `POST` bid products with `price: "abc"`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid product with price 0.

cases.title: Offering more than the requested quantity is refused
cases.why: Code 511 at the bid layer, and over-offering distorts the comparison.
cases.steps: `POST` bid products with quantity above the line item's.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid product above the requested quantity.

cases.title: Offering in a different unit is refused
cases.why: Code 512 — a unit mismatch makes every price incomparable.
cases.steps: `POST` bid products with a different unit.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing created.

cases.title: A bid on a line item from another event is refused
cases.why: Cross-event writes are the most damaging category of bid bug.
cases.steps: `POST` bid products with a `line_item_uuid` from a different event.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid product created; the other event is untouched.

cases.title: Revising a bid replaces the price and keeps history
cases.why: Revision is normal, and the *latest* value must be what ranks while the earlier one stays auditable.
cases.steps: `PATCH /bids/revise_bid/:id` with a new price.
cases.expected: 200; the current price is the new one, the old one is in history.
cases.oracle: Current price and history both as expected. ≈ BE-5.2.

cases.title: Revising a non-existent bid is refused
cases.why: Code 32 "Bid not found" — must not be a nil dereference.
cases.steps: `PATCH /bids/revise_bid/<fabricated>`.
cases.oracle: That code; no 500. ≈ BE-5.7.

cases.title: A bid in a terminal state cannot be revised
cases.why: The lookup deliberately excludes revised, rejected, selected, revoked, inactive and draft bids. Revising a *selected* bid would change an award after the fact.
cases.steps: Attempt to revise a selected bid, then a rejected one.
cases.expected: Refused both times (32).
cases.oracle: Neither bid changes.

cases.title: Rejecting a bid works only on an active bid
cases.why: Rejecting a non-active bid is meaningless and the endpoint guards it explicitly.
cases.steps: `PATCH /bids/:id/reject` on an active bid, then on an already-rejected one.
cases.expected: First succeeds; second refused (101).
cases.oracle: One rejection recorded. ≈ BE-5.3.

cases.title: Updating the status of a revoked bid is refused
cases.why: Code 151 — a revoked bid is out of the event and must stay out.
cases.steps: `PATCH /bids/update_bid_status/:id` on a revoked bid.
cases.oracle: Status unchanged.

cases.title: A vendor cannot read another vendor's bid
cases.why: PRD §7.2 at the layer where it is actually enforced (`can_view_bid?`). The UI check in UI-VBID-025 is the symptom; this is the cause.
cases.setup: Two vendors with bids.
cases.steps: As A, `GET /bids/:B_id`.
cases.expected: Refused (32).
cases.oracle: No bid payload for B — assert on the body, not only the status.

cases.title: The bid index is restricted to super admins and Procol employees
cases.why: It is a cross-vendor read by design, so its gate is the only thing standing between it and a full bid dump.
cases.steps: `GET /bids` as a normal buyer, then without `vendor_ids`.
cases.expected: Refused (101) for the buyer; 422 (5) for the missing filter.
cases.oracle: No bid list returned in either case.

cases.title: Bid feedback is restricted to the order's team or a super admin
cases.why: One of only two genuinely gated methods on an otherwise open bid policy.
cases.setup: A buyer not on the order's team and not a super admin.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/:id/feedback`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No feedback recorded. ≈ BE-5.4.

cases.title: Accepting a knockout offer twice is idempotent
cases.why: Double submission at round boundaries must not advance the round twice.
cases.setup: A live knockout auction with an open offer.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/accept_knockout_offer` twice.
cases.expected: One acceptance.
cases.oracle: One acceptance recorded; no 500. ≈ BE-5.6.

cases.title: Accepting a dutch offer validates the quantity
cases.why: Three distinct refusals live here — missing (249), non-positive (101) and below-minimum (246) — and they are easy to collapse into one.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/accept_dutch_offer` with no quantity, then `0`, then below the minimum.
cases.expected: 249, 101 and 246 respectively.
cases.oracle: Each specific code; no acceptance in any case.

cases.title: Uploading a bid Excel requires view access to the event
cases.why: A bulk write path — weak authorization here is worth more than any single-bid bypass.
cases.setup: A user without view access.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/:id/upload_bid_excel`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bids created. ≈ BE-5.8.

cases.title: Two vendors' bids coexist and rank correctly
cases.why: Everything in §11 needs two bids to award between, and ranking is the derived value the whole auction depends on.
cases.setup: A live rank auction with two invited vendors.
cases.steps: Bid 100 as A, then 90 as B. Read the buyer's view.
cases.expected: Two bids from two distinct companies; B ranks ahead of A.
cases.oracle: Two bids with **different** company ids, and the rank order as expected.

cases.title: Anomaly detection flags a wildly out-of-band bid
cases.why: It fires only with three or more bids on a line item, skips surrogate bids, and does not run for knockout, dutch or book-building — a lot of conditions to get wrong, and a false positive blocks a legitimate bid.
cases.setup: A line item with three comparable bids, then a fourth far outside the range.
cases.steps: Submit the outlier.
cases.expected: Flagged as an anomaly with a message and a suggested price, rather than silently accepted or hard-refused.
cases.oracle: The anomaly response is returned; verify a *normal* bid in the same state is not flagged.

cases.title: A staggered event refuses a non-surrogate bid on this endpoint
cases.why: Code 508 — staggered events accept bids only through their own path, and this is the guard that keeps the two apart.
cases.setup: A staggered event.
cases.steps: `POST /v1/bids` as a vendor.
cases.oracle: No bid created.

cases.title: A buyer places a surrogate RFQ bid for a vendor
cases.why: The core capability. It must land as a bid attributed to the vendor, not to the buyer.
cases.setup: A live RFQ stage with a vendor invited; the caller is the event's creator.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` with the vendor's `company_id` and the trade.
cases.expected: 200; a bid for that vendor.
cases.oracle: The bid's `company_id` is the vendor's and it is flagged as a surrogate bid. `flows/surrogate.ts`.

cases.title: A buyer places a surrogate technical response for a vendor
cases.why: The technical half, with its own endpoint and its own payload covering both the global and line-item forms.
cases.setup: A live RFP stage with a vendor invited.
cases.steps: `POST /template_responses/create_surrogate_response` with both forms' pages.
cases.expected: 200; a submitted response attributed to the vendor.
cases.oracle: The response exists for that vendor and is marked surrogate.

cases.title: A surrogate bid is refused on an offline-trading event
cases.why: The recognition logic explicitly excludes offline trading, so the call falls through to the normal path and is refused as a self-company bid.
cases.setup: An offline-trade stage.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` as the buyer.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid created.

cases.title: A surrogate bid is refused when the company config forbids it
cases.why: Code 10. Some organisations bar it on principle and honouring that is a compliance requirement, not a preference.
cases.setup: An event whose config sets `is_buyer_not_allowed_to_add_surrogate_bid`.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input`.
cases.oracle: No bid created.

cases.title: A buyer who is not a valid surrogate bidder is refused
cases.why: Code 165. The permitted set is super admin, valid bidding team, or the event's creator — anyone else placing bids for vendors is a serious problem.
cases.setup: A buyer in the company but none of those three.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input`.
cases.oracle: No bid created.

cases.title: The event's creator can place a surrogate bid
cases.why: The positive half of API-SUR-005; without it the gate could be refusing everyone.
cases.setup: The event's creator, not a super admin, not on a bidding team.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input`.
cases.expected: Accepted.
cases.oracle: Bid created for the vendor.

cases.title: A surrogate bid is accepted on an Upcoming event
cases.why: Deliberately wider than a vendor's own window — a buyer records a bid received offline before the event opens. Contrast with API-BID-005.
cases.setup: An Upcoming event.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input`.
cases.expected: Accepted.
cases.oracle: Bid created while a vendor's own bid on the same stage is refused with 33.

cases.title: After expiry, a surrogate bid depends on the post-expiry setting
cases.why: It is the only setting that permits a bid after the window closed, which makes it the highest-integrity switch in this section.
cases.setup: A closed event, on a tenant with the setting off and one with it on.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` on each.
cases.expected: Refused (33) where off; accepted where on.
cases.oracle: Both outcomes, and where accepted the bid is marked surrogate.

cases.title: A surrogate bid for a vendor who already bid is refused by default
cases.why: Code 99. Overwriting a vendor's own bid is the most damaging thing this feature could do, and it is refused unless a specific config allows it.
cases.setup: A vendor with their own active bid; no `allowed_surrogate_bid_even_after_bid`.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` for them.
cases.oracle: The vendor's own bid is unchanged.

cases.title: With the config on, a repeat surrogate bid revises rather than duplicates
cases.why: With `allowed_surrogate_bid_even_after_bid`, an existing surrogate bid is *returned for revision* instead of a second one being created. A duplicate would double-count the vendor in the comparison.
cases.setup: gate: `allowed_surrogate_bid_even_after_bid`. A vendor with an existing surrogate bid.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` again at a new price.
cases.expected: One bid, at the new price, with history.
cases.oracle: Bid count for that vendor is still 1. `bids_controller_helper.rb:2670-2677`.

cases.title: Reading surrogate approval flows requires approval-read permission
cases.why: One of only two genuinely gated bid-policy methods. An empty list would read as "no approval needed" and let the bid straight through, so a refusal is the correct behaviour and an empty 200 is a finding.
cases.setup: A buyer without approval-flow read permission.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/approval_workflows_for_surrogate_bid_create`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: A refusal, not an empty array. ≈ BE-5.5.

cases.title: The approval-flow lookup requires a trade request id
cases.why: Code 2 — a missing id must not be a nil dereference.
cases.steps: `POST` the same endpoint with no `trade_request_id`.
cases.expected: 422, code 2.
cases.oracle: That code; no 500.

cases.title: The approval-flow lookup applies the surrogate permission checks too
cases.why: It runs the same `allowed_surrogate_bid_placement` guard, so a buyer barred from surrogate bidding must not be able to enumerate the approval flows either.
cases.setup: A buyer refused by API-SUR-005.
cases.steps: `POST` the approval-flow endpoint.
cases.expected: The same refusal.
cases.oracle: Same error code as the bid attempt.

cases.title: A surrogate bid requiring approval enters a requested state
cases.why: On approval-configured tenants the bid does not count yet, and a test asserting an active bid fails there permanently.
cases.setup: gate: surrogate-bid approval configured.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` with approval remarks.
cases.expected: The bid is approval-requested; an approval record carries the remarks.
cases.oracle: Bid status approval-requested; remarks stored.

cases.title: A surrogate bid is exempt from anomaly detection
cases.why: Anomaly detection deliberately skips surrogate bids; if it did not, a buyer recording a genuinely low offline quote would be blocked.
cases.setup: Three comparable bids and a surrogate bid far outside the range.
cases.steps: Place the surrogate bid.
cases.expected: Accepted without an anomaly flag.
cases.oracle: No anomaly response; the same price as a vendor's own bid *is* flagged.

cases.title: A surrogate bid picks up the vendor's first make where makes exist
cases.why: When the vendor has alternative makes, the surrogate path assigns the first one automatically. Without it the bid is unattributable to a make and the comparison is incomplete.
cases.setup: A vendor with alternatives mapped on the event group.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` without an alternatives mapping.
cases.expected: The bid carries the vendor's first active make.
cases.oracle: The mapping id on the bid equals the lowest-id active mapping for that vendor.

cases.title: A surrogate bid validates prices exactly like a vendor's
cases.why: The surrogate path must not be the lenient one — a negative price entered by a buyer is as wrong as one entered by a vendor.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` with a negative price, a negative quantity and a negative GST in turn.
cases.expected: 106, 35 and 107 respectively.
cases.oracle: Nothing created in any case.

cases.title: A surrogate bid with no products is refused
cases.why: Buyer-added bids are exempt from *some* product validation, so this case establishes what the exemption actually covers rather than assuming it covers everything.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` with no trade products.
cases.expected: Refused, or accepted-and-documented — with the resulting state recorded.
cases.oracle: Record the behaviour; if a bid with no products becomes active, that is a finding worth raising against `bid.rb:216-222`'s `is_buyer_added_bid?` exemption.

cases.title: A surrogate bid is distinguishable from a vendor's own bid
cases.why: At award time it matters enormously which is which. If the flag is not set, the audit trail is gone.
cases.setup: One vendor bid and one surrogate bid on the same event.
cases.steps: Read both.
cases.expected: Exactly one is marked as a surrogate/buyer-added bid.
cases.oracle: The flag differs between the two.

cases.title: A buyer-edited bid is labelled as such
cases.why: `BidContextLabelService` stamps a `buyer_edit` context, and that label is what a later auditor reads.
cases.setup: A vendor's bid, edited by the buyer.
cases.steps: `PATCH` the bid as the buyer.
cases.expected: The bid carries a buyer-edit context entry.
cases.oracle: The context's latest key is a buyer-edit key.

cases.title: A surrogate bid cannot be placed for a vendor who is not on the event
cases.why: Otherwise the buyer could manufacture a bid from an uninvited company.
cases.steps: `POST /bids/template_input` with a company that is not on the audience.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No bid created for that company.

cases.title: A surrogate bid appears in the vendor's own view
cases.why: If the vendor cannot see it they may bid again, and the two records disagree. Whatever the product's intent, the state must be honest.
cases.setup: A surrogate bid placed for a vendor.
cases.steps: As that vendor, read their bids on the event.
cases.expected: The bid is visible with its price.
cases.oracle: The vendor's read returns a bid at that price.

cases.title: An active RFQ converts to an auction
cases.why: The happy path, and it is the only way to reach knockout and dutch strategies at all.
cases.setup: A published RFQ with bids.
cases.steps: `PATCH /trade/move_to_auction` with the RFQ's trade id and an auction config.
cases.expected: 200; a new auction trade as a child of the RFQ.
cases.oracle: The new trade's `parent_id` is the RFQ's id. ≈ BE-7.1.

cases.title: Converting the same RFQ twice is refused
cases.why: Code 94. The model enforces at most one non-cancelled auction per `(parent_id, event_group_id)`, and a second one would split the event's bids.
cases.steps: Convert, then convert again.
cases.oracle: Still exactly one auction child. ≈ BE-7.2.

cases.title: Converting a non-existent trade is refused
cases.why: Code 95 — the first guard, and it must not be a nil dereference.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with a fabricated trade id.
cases.oracle: That code. ≈ BE-7.3.

cases.title: Converting on a superseded event version is refused
cases.why: Code 101 — the same staleness rule as publish, on a path that creates a new trade.
cases.setup: An RFQ whose event group has a newer version.
cases.steps: `PATCH move_to_auction`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No auction created. ≈ BE-7.4.

cases.title: Converting an already-auctioning trade is refused
cases.why: Code 93 "Trade is already of auction type" — distinct from the duplicate-child guard, and reached by a different route.
cases.steps: `PATCH move_to_auction` on an auction.
cases.oracle: That specific code, not 94. ≈ BE-7.5.

cases.title: A caller from neither the owning nor the broker company is refused
cases.why: The company check is separate from the policy check, and brokers are a legitimate third party — so the rule is narrower than "same company".
cases.setup: A caller from an unrelated company with create permission.
cases.steps: `PATCH move_to_auction`.
cases.expected: Refused (101).
cases.oracle: No auction created. ≈ BE-7.6.

cases.title: Conversion requires both create permission and view access
cases.why: `move_to_auction?` is `create? && allowed_to_view_event?` — two independent gates, and passing one is not enough.
cases.setup: A user with create permission but no view access to this event, and the reverse.
cases.steps: `PATCH move_to_auction` as each.
cases.expected: Both refused.
cases.oracle: No auction created in either case.

cases.title: A line-item to lot closing-mode switch on a multi-product trade is refused
cases.why: Code 503, "You cannot award entire lot when RFQ was done for partial lot." — a genuine commercial constraint, not a technical one.
cases.setup: A multi-product RFQ run as line-item.
cases.steps: `PATCH move_to_auction` with `auction_closing_mode: lot`.
cases.oracle: No auction created. ≈ BE-7.8.

cases.title: Fast bidding requires more than one active or closed trade product
cases.why: Code 798 — "CBD mode requires at least two active line items."
cases.setup: A single-product RFQ.
cases.steps: `PATCH move_to_auction` with fast bidding enabled.
cases.oracle: No auction created. ≈ BE-7.7.

cases.title: Rank-based tenants validate the start and end prices
cases.why: `validate_start_and_end_price` runs only for rank-enabled companies, so an invalid pair passes silently elsewhere and is caught here.
cases.setup: gate: `rfx_project_enabled` (rank-based). An invalid start/end pair.
cases.steps: `PATCH move_to_auction`.
cases.expected: Refused with the price-validation error.
cases.oracle: No auction created.

cases.title: The RFQ becomes bid-restricted once its auction exists
cases.why: Code 769. It is the state change conversion makes to the *parent*, and it is easy to overlook because the new auction is what everyone looks at.
cases.steps: Convert, then attempt a bid on the RFQ.
cases.expected: Refused with 769.
cases.oracle: That specific code.

cases.title: The RFQ's bids survive the conversion
cases.why: They are the baseline the auction's savings are computed against; losing them changes every number afterwards.
cases.steps: Convert an RFQ that had two bids. Read the RFQ.
cases.expected: Both bids still present and readable.
cases.oracle: Bid count on the RFQ unchanged.

cases.title: A proposal is created for an eligible company
cases.why: The first of the four calls, and the one the gate applies to.
cases.setup: A closed event with at least one submitted bid.
cases.steps: `POST /proposal` with the event group.
cases.expected: 200 with a proposal uuid, in draft.
cases.oracle: Uuid returned; status draft. ≈ BE-6.1. `flows/awarding.ts`.

cases.title: An award response allocates a line item to a vendor
cases.why: It is the actual allocation; a proposal with no responses awards nothing.
cases.setup: A draft proposal and a submitted bid on the line item.
cases.steps: `POST /proposal/:uuid/add_response` with the vendor, line item and quantity.
cases.expected: 200; the allocation is on the proposal.
cases.oracle: The proposal's responses contain that vendor and quantity.

cases.title: Adding a response with no submitted bid is refused
cases.why: Awarding a vendor who never bid is the clearest possible integrity failure in this section.
cases.setup: A vendor with no bid.
cases.steps: `POST add_response` for them.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No allocation created for that vendor.

cases.title: The approval workflow is readable for a proposal
cases.why: Submission needs the flow's uuid, so an empty or wrong flow makes submission impossible — and a *silently* empty one makes it look approved.
cases.steps: `GET /proposal/:uuid/approval_workflows`.
cases.expected: At least one flow with steps and approvers.
cases.oracle: A flow uuid and at least one approver uuid.

cases.title: Submitting the proposal moves it to requested and blocks further awarding
cases.why: PRD §3.5 — the award goes through a proposal and an approval workflow, and one event must not carry two live proposals.
cases.steps: `POST /proposal/:uuid/submit` with the approval flow uuid. Then attempt a second proposal.
cases.expected: Submitted; the second proposal is refused.
cases.oracle: `should_allow_awarding` is false afterwards. ≈ BE-6.2.

cases.title: Awarding is blocked while the caller holds a draft proposal
cases.why: The gate is per-user for drafts, which is subtly different from the selected/requested rule.
cases.setup: The same buyer with a draft proposal.
cases.steps: `POST /proposal` again.
cases.expected: Refused, or `should_allow_awarding` already false.
cases.oracle: Proposal count unchanged. ≈ BE-6.3.

cases.title: Discarding a draft proposal re-enables awarding
cases.why: It is the escape hatch from API-AWD-006 and it must actually clear the flag.
cases.steps: Discard the draft. Re-read the event group.
cases.expected: `should_allow_awarding` is true again.
cases.oracle: The flag flips back; a new proposal can be created. ≈ BE-6.6.

cases.title: Awarding is blocked before the close window is reached
cases.why: Awarding while bidding is still legally open would cut off bids that were still permitted.
cases.setup: A live event whose latest commercial stage has not reached its close window.
cases.steps: Read `config.should_allow_awarding`; attempt a proposal.
cases.expected: The flag is false and the proposal is refused.
cases.oracle: Both. `event_group_controller_helper.rb:629-648`.

cases.title: A caller from another company cannot add a response
cases.why: `add_response?` is the policy method behind show, submit and the approval lookup, so a hole here opens four endpoints at once.
cases.setup: A caller whose allowed companies exclude the proposal's company.
cases.steps: `POST add_response`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No allocation created. ≈ BE-6.5.

cases.title: A Procol employee passes the proposal policy unconditionally
cases.why: A deliberate support back door; it must work for them and for nobody else.
cases.setup: A Procol employee.
cases.steps: `GET /proposal/:id`.
cases.expected: Allowed.
cases.oracle: Readable; then confirm a non-employee outside the company is refused.

cases.title: Creating a contract form requires the contract-creation config
cases.why: It is an extra gate on top of `add_response?` and it is tenant-specific.
cases.setup: A workspace without `is_contract_creation_enabled`.
cases.steps: `POST /proposal/:uuid/create_contract_form`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No contract form created. ≈ BE-6.4.

cases.title: Partial awarding splits a line item across vendors and the quantities add up
cases.why: It is why line-item awarding exists, and the arithmetic is what gets billed.
cases.setup: A line item of 100 with two bids.
cases.steps: `add_response` 60 to A and 40 to B, then submit.
cases.expected: Both allocations recorded; total awarded = 100.
cases.oracle: Sum of awarded quantities equals the requested quantity; neither vendor exceeds their offered quantity.

cases.title: Awarding more than the requested quantity is refused
cases.why: Over-awarding creates a commitment the requisition never covered.
cases.steps: `add_response` 60 and 60 on a quantity of 100.
cases.expected: The second is refused.
cases.oracle: Total awarded never exceeds 100.

cases.title: Awarding more than a vendor offered is refused
cases.why: A vendor who offered 40 cannot be awarded 60; the validation is per-vendor, not just per-line.
cases.setup: A vendor who offered 40.
cases.steps: `add_response` 60 for them.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No allocation above the offered quantity.

cases.title: Awarding a zero or negative quantity is refused
cases.why: PRD §5's positive-quantity rule, at the last step where it matters.
cases.steps: `add_response` with `0`, then `-10`.
cases.expected: Refused both times.
cases.oracle: No allocation created.

cases.title: Closing the bid to select a winner is refused outside the window
cases.why: Code 9, "Unable to close the order at this time. Please wait for the bidding to end."
cases.setup: A live event inside its window.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/:id/close_bid`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No winner selected. ≈ BE-6.7.

cases.title: Closing the bid selects the winning bid
cases.why: The positive half; it is what actually marks a bid selected.
cases.setup: A closed event with bids.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/:id/close_bid` naming the winning bid.
cases.expected: That bid becomes selected.
cases.oracle: The bid's status is selected and no other bid is.

cases.title: A selected bid can no longer be revised
cases.why: It is the guarantee that an award is final; revision after selection would change the awarded price.
cases.steps: Attempt `PATCH /bids/revise_bid/:id` on the selected bid.
cases.expected: Refused (32).
cases.oracle: The selected bid's price is unchanged.

cases.title: The awarding sheet downloads for a valid uuid and is refused for an invalid one
cases.why: It is a data-export endpoint; a permissive one leaks a whole event's commercials.
cases.steps: `GET /reports/download_awarding_sheet/:uuid` with a valid uuid, then a fabricated one, then another company's.
cases.expected: The first succeeds; the others are refused.
cases.oracle: No file content in the refused cases. ≈ BE-6.8.

cases.title: The awarded event reports its awarded state consistently
cases.why: Several read paths derive from the award; if they disagree, the buyer and the vendor see different outcomes.
cases.steps: After the award, read the event group, the stage and the bid.
cases.expected: All three agree on the awarded vendor and quantity.
cases.oracle: Three-way consistency check.

cases.title: The full chain runs end to end
cases.why: It is the acceptance test for PRD §3 as a whole, and it is what the existing suite already drives — create, publish, bid, award.
cases.setup: A buyer, a vendor, and a live event.
cases.steps: Create the draft → create the stage(s) → activate → vendor technical response → vendor bid → close → proposal → response → approval flow → submit.
cases.expected: Every step succeeds and the event ends awarded to the bidding vendor.
cases.oracle: Assert each step's own oracle, and finally that the awarded vendor equals the vendor who bid.

cases.title: A rejected proposal returns the event to awardable
cases.why: Otherwise a rejection deadlocks the event and there is no route out.
cases.setup: A submitted proposal.
cases.steps: Reject it through the approval workflow. Re-read the event group.
cases.expected: `should_allow_awarding` is true; a new proposal can be created.
cases.oracle: The flag and a successful new proposal.

cases.title: Withdrawing an active event requires a remark and succeeds
cases.why: It is the buyer's emergency stop, and the remark is the audit trail vendors are shown.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "withdrawn"` and `withdraw_remark: {remarks, attachments}`.
cases.expected: 200; status withdrawn.
cases.oracle: Status withdrawn and the remark stored. ≈ BE-2.17.

cases.title: Withdrawing with blank remarks is refused
cases.why: Without it, an event can vanish for vendors with no explanation.
cases.steps: `PATCH` with `status: "withdrawn"` and empty remarks.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Status unchanged. ≈ BE-2.18.

cases.title: Withdrawal notifies vendors exactly once
cases.why: The mail fires on the status transition; two mails is a support call and none leaves vendors bidding on a dead event.
cases.steps: Withdraw, then re-issue the withdrawal.
cases.expected: One notification overall.
cases.oracle: Count the enqueued mail jobs across both calls. ≈ BE-9.2.

cases.title: Withdrawing twice is idempotent
cases.why: Retries happen; a second withdrawal record would corrupt the history.
cases.steps: `PATCH` withdrawn twice.
cases.expected: One withdrawal.
cases.oracle: One remark, one status change.

cases.title: Activating a withdrawn event is refused
cases.why: Resurrecting a withdrawn event reopens bidding vendors were told was over.
cases.steps: `PATCH` a withdrawn event with `status: "active"`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Status stays withdrawn. ≈ BE-9.1.

cases.title: Withdrawal releases the PR's in-progress quantity
cases.why: `update_in_progress_quantity` fires on the withdrawn transition; without it a withdrawn event permanently consumes the requisition.
cases.setup: A PR-linked published event.
cases.steps: Withdraw it. Read the PR.
cases.expected: The quantity returns to open.
cases.oracle: PR open quantity back to its pre-event value.

cases.title: An active event can be cloned
cases.why: It is how buyers run a recurring event, and its policy has four separate refusal conditions.
cases.steps: `POST /event_groups/:uuid/create_clone`.
cases.expected: 200; a new draft with the same line items and configuration.
cases.oracle: New event group with matching line items and a different ref id.

cases.title: A withdrawn event can be cloned
cases.why: Deliberately allowed — cloning is how a buyer relaunches an event they had to pull.
cases.steps: `POST create_clone` on a withdrawn event.
cases.expected: Allowed.
cases.oracle: A new draft exists.
