cases.title: Cloning a draft is refused
cases.why: Code 1122, "Only active or withdrawn events can be cloned."
cases.steps: `POST create_clone` on a draft.
cases.oracle: No clone created. ≈ BE-8.3.

cases.title: Cloning a PR-created event is refused
cases.why: Code 1123 — the clone would have no requisition behind it.
cases.steps: `POST create_clone` on a PR-created event.
cases.oracle: No clone created. ≈ BE-8.4.

cases.title: A planner cannot clone
cases.why: A policy carve-out that would otherwise pass because cloning needs only create permission.
cases.setup: A planner with create permission.
cases.steps: `POST create_clone`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No clone created. ≈ BE-8.2.

cases.title: An amendment publish requires non-blank remarks
cases.why: An amendment changes what vendors bid against; the remark is what they are shown.
cases.setup: An amendment draft.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate with blank `amendment_remarks.remarks`, then with real ones.
cases.expected: First refused, second published.
cases.oracle: The amendment is recorded with the remark text. ≈ BE-2.20.

cases.title: An amendment publish with the remarks key absent does not crash
cases.why: The amendment-draft path reads that key directly, so an absent one is a nil-dereference candidate.
cases.steps: `PATCH` to activate an amendment draft with no `amendment_remarks` at all.
cases.expected: A readable refusal.

cases.title: Ownership changes for the owner, a super admin or a Procol employee, and nobody else
cases.why: It is how an event survives someone leaving the company, and it hands over full control — so the gate matters as much as the feature.
cases.steps: `POST /event_groups/:uuid/change_ownership` as the owner, as a super admin, and as an unrelated buyer.
cases.expected: First two allowed, the third refused.
cases.oracle: Owner reflected after the allowed calls; unchanged after the refusal. ≈ BE-4.10, BE-4.11.

cases.title: `GET /api/event_groups` requires trade read permission
cases.why: The listing is the module's front door.
cases.steps: List as a user with trade read, then as one without.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: Both outcomes.

cases.title: `GET /api/event_groups/:id` requires read *and* a visible stage
cases.why: Two conditions, and the second is the one people forget — a user with read access and no visible stage is refused.
cases.steps: Read as the owner, then as a user with trade read but no stage visibility.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: No event payload in the refusal. ≈ BE-8.1.

cases.title: `POST /api/event_groups` requires trade create permission
cases.why: The privileged write in the module.
cases.steps: Create with and without the permission.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One event group created in total. ≈ BE-1.7.

cases.title: Stage creation requires create permission *and* sourcing-events access
cases.why: Two independent gates; a user can pass the first and fail the second, which is a real configuration.
cases.steps: `POST /trade/template_input` as a user with both, then with only create.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One stage created in total. ≈ BE-8.7.

cases.title: Stage update allows a Procol employee unconditionally
cases.why: A support back door, and back doors need their own cases so nobody removes them accidentally — or widens them.
cases.steps: `PATCH /trade/:id` as a Procol employee outside the company.
cases.expected: Allowed.
cases.oracle: The update applies; then confirm a non-employee outside the company is refused.

cases.title: Vendor-onboarding-v2 stage updates need the onboarding permission
cases.why: A mode-specific extra gate that a generic stage-update test would miss entirely.
cases.setup: A vendor-onboarding-v2 stage and a user without that permission.
cases.steps: `PATCH /trade/:id`.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No update applied. ≈ BE-8.6.

cases.title: Event-group update accepts either policy branch and refuses outside both
cases.why: The policy is a two-branch OR (Procol CSM, or allowed-company plus trade create). Testing one branch proves half a rule.
cases.steps: `PATCH` as a CSM Procol employee, as an in-company buyer with create, and as a user in neither category.
cases.expected: First two allowed, third refused.
cases.oracle: All three outcomes.

cases.title: Clone requires allowed company, create permission, non-planner, non-draft, non-PR
cases.why: Five conditions on one endpoint; each is its own way in.
cases.steps: Vary one condition at a time from a known-good clone.
cases.expected: The good case succeeds; each variation is refused.
cases.oracle: Exactly one clone created across the whole set.

cases.title: Vendor self-participation requires show access and open tenders
cases.why: `participate?` is `show? && open_tenders?` — again two conditions.
cases.steps: Participate as an invited vendor on an open-tender event, then as an uninvited vendor, then on a non-open-tender event.
cases.expected: First allowed, other two refused.
cases.oracle: One audience row created in total.

cases.title: `update_egli` needs stage-update rights *and* the evaluation window
cases.why: The policy allows it while the inline time check still refuses — two layers, and a test that only has permission passes wrongly.
cases.steps: Call it with rights inside the window, with rights outside it, and without rights inside it.
cases.expected: Only the first succeeds.
cases.oracle: Evaluators change exactly once. ≈ BE-3.5.

cases.title: Bid feedback needs the order's team or super admin plus the config
cases.why: One of the two genuinely gated bid-policy methods.
cases.steps: Add feedback as a team member, then as an outsider.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One feedback record. ≈ BE-5.4.

cases.title: Surrogate approval-flow reads need approval-flow read permission
cases.why: The other gated bid-policy method, and an empty list would read as "no approval needed".
cases.steps: Call it with and without the permission.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused — not an empty success.
cases.oracle: Both outcomes. ≈ BE-5.5.

cases.title: Proposal endpoints all sit behind `add_response?`
cases.why: Show, submit, the approval lookup and discard share one policy method — so one hole opens four endpoints.
cases.steps: Call each of the four as a caller outside the allowed companies.
cases.expected: All four refused.
cases.oracle: Four refusals; no proposal state changes.

cases.title: Contract-form creation needs `add_response?` *and* the tenant config
cases.why: A config gate stacked on a policy gate.
cases.steps: Call it with the policy satisfied and the config off.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No contract form. ≈ BE-6.4.

cases.title: Live-auction audience edits need view access
cases.why: A narrow gate on a write that changes who can bid.
cases.steps: Add an audience with and without view access.
cases.expected: Allowed, then refused.
cases.oracle: One audience row. ≈ BE-4.9.

cases.title: Restricted admin operations are limited to an explicit allow-list
cases.why: Some maintenance endpoints are restricted to named Procol employees; an allow-list that stops being enforced is a privileged-access failure.
cases.steps: Call the restricted operation as a non-listed Procol employee.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing regenerated or changed. ≈ BE-8.8.

cases.title: A vendor cannot call any buyer write endpoint
cases.why: A sweep rather than a single case — it is the cheapest way to catch a newly added endpoint with no policy.
cases.steps: As a vendor session, call event-group create/update, stage create, proposal create and close_bid.
cases.expected: All refused.
cases.oracle: Nothing created by any of them; add new write endpoints to this sweep as they appear.

cases.title: Every 403/422 refusal leaks nothing about the resource
cases.why: A refusal that echoes the event's title or the vendor's name is an information leak dressed as an authorization success.
cases.steps: Collect the bodies of ten refusals from this section.
cases.expected: Each carries a code and a generic message only.
cases.oracle: No titles, vendor names or prices in any refusal body.

cases.title: Every required parameter is enforced on every write endpoint
cases.why: It is the broadest requirement in the PRD; a systematic sweep beats one case per field.
cases.steps: For event-group create/update, stage create, bid create and proposal create: omit each required parameter in turn.
cases.expected: 422 with code 2 (or the endpoint's specific code) each time.
cases.oracle: Nothing created in any variation.

cases.title: Unknown parameters are ignored, not persisted
cases.why: An endpoint that stores whatever it is sent is a mass-assignment risk.
cases.steps: Send `{"is_admin": true, "company_id": <another company>}` alongside a valid create.
cases.expected: Created, with those values ignored.
cases.oracle: The created row's company is the caller's own.

cases.title: A malformed body type is refused, not coerced
cases.why: PRD §5's "no partial record" clause.
cases.steps: Send `line_items` as a string, `config` as an array, `quantity` as an object where a number belongs.
cases.expected: 4xx with a readable message each time.
cases.oracle: No 500; nothing created. ≈ BE-1.12.

cases.title: Invalid JSON is refused cleanly
cases.why: The framework's default answer to broken JSON is easy to leave as a 500.
cases.steps: `POST` a truncated JSON body.
cases.expected: A 4xx.
cases.oracle: Not a 500.

cases.title: A fabricated uuid is refused with a not-found code
cases.why: Every id-taking endpoint should answer 533/95/32/250 as appropriate rather than raising.
cases.steps: Call event-group show/update, trade show, bid show and proposal show with fabricated ids.
cases.expected: The appropriate not-found code each time.
cases.oracle: No 500 in any case.

cases.title: An id of the wrong type is refused
cases.why: `"abc"` or `null` where an integer or uuid belongs is a classic 500.
cases.steps: Call the same endpoints with `"abc"`, `null` and `-1`.
cases.expected: 4xx each time.

cases.title: Another company's id is refused, not treated as not-found
cases.why: The distinction matters: "not found" for a resource that exists elsewhere is acceptable, but succeeding is a cross-tenant breach.
cases.steps: Read and update company B's event group from a company A session.
cases.expected: Refused.
cases.oracle: No payload and no write.

cases.title: Very long strings are bounded politely
cases.why: PRD §6. An unbounded string field becomes a database error, which becomes a 500.
cases.steps: Send a 100,000-character title, description and clause.
cases.expected: Either accepted or refused with a stated limit. No 500, no silent truncation.
cases.oracle: Compare the stored value to what was sent.

cases.title: Emoji and multi-byte text round-trip byte for byte
cases.why: Four-byte characters are where encoding and column charset assumptions break.
cases.steps: Create an event with emoji and CJK text in the title and a line-item description. Read it back.
cases.expected: Byte-identical.
cases.oracle: Exact equality on read-back, and again in the database. ≈ PRD §6.

cases.title: Numeric edge values are handled or refused explicitly
cases.why: `0`, huge values, high precision and `e`-notation each fail differently.
cases.steps: Send `0`, `999999999999.99`, `1e10`, `0.000001` as prices and quantities.
cases.expected: Each either accepted with the exact value preserved or refused with a message.
cases.oracle: The stored value equals the sent value wherever accepted.

cases.title: Epoch times outside a sane range are refused
cases.why: Schedules take epoch seconds; `0` and year-3000 values would create events nobody can bid on and reports nobody can read.
cases.steps: Send `bid_start_time: 0`, a negative value, and a value 100 years out.
cases.expected: Refused, or accepted with a documented clamp.
cases.oracle: No schedule row with an absurd time.

cases.title: Epoch times as strings are handled consistently
cases.why: Clients send `"1757404800"` as often as the integer; silently parsing one and not the other creates a phantom scheduling bug.
cases.steps: Send both forms.
cases.expected: Both accepted identically, or the string refused with a message.
cases.oracle: The resulting schedules are identical, or the refusal is explicit.

cases.title: A script payload in a text field is stored inert
cases.why: Event titles reach every invited vendor's screen — stored XSS here has the widest blast radius in the product.
cases.steps: Create an event whose title is ``. Read it as the buyer and as a vendor.
cases.expected: Stored and returned as text.
cases.oracle: The response is escaped or plainly text; the UI counterpart is UI-VAL-003.

cases.title: SQL-ish input is treated as data
cases.why: The cheapest probe for a whole class of failure, and search endpoints are the usual place it is missed.
cases.steps: Send `'; DROP TABLE event_groups; --` to product search, vendor search and the events filter.
cases.expected: Empty or literal results; no error.
cases.oracle: Normal responses; the table still exists (a subsequent read succeeds).

cases.title: Duplicate creation requests do not produce duplicate events
cases.why: A retried create is the most common client behaviour on a slow network.
cases.steps: Send the identical create twice.
cases.expected: Either one event, or two with distinct ids and a documented behaviour.
cases.oracle: Record which; if two events result, flag it as a finding for the UI's double-submit case (UI-PUB-007).

cases.title: A concurrent double activation produces one published event
cases.why: The `lock_transaction` on this endpoint exists for it — and a double-render on a held lock is the top-ranked cause of the standing 500.
cases.steps: Fire two activations for the same event group simultaneously.
cases.expected: One activation; the other refused with a lock/conflict code.
cases.oracle: One set of stages and audiences. If the loser returns an untyped 500, that confirms the double-render candidate — record the exception class.

cases.title: A duplicate user email is refused on user create
cases.why: PRD §6, and duplicated identities break team-based permissions.
cases.steps: `POST /users/create_user` twice with the same email.
cases.expected: The second refused with a readable message.
cases.oracle: One user. `flows/masterData.ts`.

cases.title: The phone rule is verified against the PRD's stated criterion
cases.why: The PRD states "any 10-digit number, stored with a `+91` prefix by default" **and explicitly asks QA to verify the claim**. If the product is stricter or looser, the difference is the deliverable.
cases.steps: `POST /users/create_user` with `9876543210`, `1234567890`, `0000000000`, a 9-digit and an 11-digit number.
cases.expected: All 10-digit values accepted and stored as `+91…`; 9 and 11 digits refused.
cases.oracle: Record the stored value for each input and diff against the specified rule. This case is expected to produce a finding either way.

cases.title: A created event group exists as a row
cases.why: It is the PRD requirement in its most literal form.
cases.steps: Create a draft. Query `event_groups` by uuid.
cases.expected: One row with status draft and the caller's company and user.
cases.oracle: Row present with those columns. `src/db/verify.ts`.

cases.title: The event group belongs to the acting workspace
cases.why: For a multi-company user, the wrong `company_id` writes an event into another tenant.
cases.steps: Create as a multi-company user in company A. Read the row.
cases.expected: `company_id` is A.
cases.oracle: Column equals A's id.

cases.title: The reference id is assigned and unique
cases.why: `add_ref_id` uses `update_columns`, bypassing validations — so uniqueness is not enforced by the model.
cases.steps: Create three events. Read their ref ids.
cases.expected: Three non-null, distinct ids.
cases.oracle: Distinctness across the three.

cases.title: Line-item rows carry their serial numbers and statuses
cases.why: Serials order the sheet and the award; statuses drive every read filter.
cases.steps: Create two line items. Read `event_group_line_items`.
cases.expected: Two active rows with serials 1 and 2.
cases.oracle: Rows, serials and statuses.

cases.title: A published stage has a bidding-time schedule row with a non-null end time
cases.why: It is the row whose absence is the top suspect for the activation 500, and `end_time` is `NOT NULL` at the database level.
cases.steps: Publish. Query `trade_schedules` for the stage.
cases.expected: A bidding-time row with both times set.
cases.oracle: Row present; `end_time` not null. This is the definitive form of API-STG-014.

cases.title: Audience rows are unique per company, item and visibility while active
cases.why: The model's own invariant, and duplicate active rows double-count a vendor everywhere downstream.
cases.steps: Publish, then re-publish. Query `audiences`.
cases.expected: One active row per company per stage.
cases.oracle: No duplicate `(audience_id, item_id, item_type, visible)` among active rows.

cases.title: A submitted bid and its products are persisted with the right prices
cases.why: The bid is the commercial artefact; if the row disagrees with the API response, the award is built on the wrong number.
cases.steps: Submit a bid. Query the bid and its products.
cases.expected: One active bid with one product row per line item, prices as submitted.
cases.oracle: Row-level equality with the submitted payload.

cases.title: A withdrawn event's status and remark are persisted
cases.why: The remark is the audit trail and it lives in the row, not in the response.
cases.steps: Withdraw. Query the event group.
cases.expected: Status withdrawn with the remark stored.
cases.oracle: Status column and remark content.

cases.title: A voided stage is marked void and stays out of every read
cases.why: `void` means "remove from everywhere" — a void stage that still appears in a read is a ghost that can accept bids.
cases.steps: Publish two of three stages. Query the third.
cases.expected: Status void; absent from every API read.
cases.oracle: Row status and API absence together.

cases.title: Nothing is written when a create or activation is refused
cases.why: PRD §5's "no partial record" clause, verified where it actually matters. During the activation regression this was the one reassuring fact: nothing was written.
cases.steps: For five refusal paths in this file, count the relevant rows before and after.
cases.expected: Identical counts.
cases.oracle: Row counts for `event_groups`, `event_group_line_items`, `trade_requests`, `trade_schedules`, `audiences` and `bids` unchanged.

cases.title: The events listing responds inside the performance budget
cases.why: PRD §7.1, measured at the API layer where the number is clean.
cases.steps: `GET /api/event_groups` on tenants with ~10, ~100 and ~1000 events.
cases.expected: Under ~3 seconds throughout.
cases.oracle: Record the three timings and trend them.

cases.title: Activating a 500-line-item event completes
cases.why: PRD §6's large-event case at the heaviest write in the module.
cases.setup: A BOQ event with 500 line items.
cases.steps: Activate and time it.
cases.expected: Completes without a timeout.
cases.oracle: 200 within the client's timeout; record the duration.

cases.title: Reading an event with 500 line items and 100 bids stays usable
cases.why: The show action builds the whole project payload — widgets, layers, proposals, approvals — and it is where a large event first becomes unusable.
cases.steps: `GET /api/event_groups/:id` on such an event.
cases.expected: A complete response in reasonable time.
cases.oracle: Response completeness and duration recorded.

cases.title: Concurrent bids from many vendors are all recorded
cases.why: An auction's last minute *is* a concurrency test, and a lost bid is a lost vendor.
cases.steps: Submit bids from 20 vendors simultaneously on one stage.
cases.expected: All 20 recorded, correctly ranked.
cases.oracle: 20 bid rows; ranks consistent with the prices.

cases.title: Rate limiting, if present, answers with a code rather than a 500
cases.why: A suite that trips a rate limit should be able to tell that apart from a real failure.
cases.steps: Issue a burst of reads.
cases.expected: Either all succeed or a rate-limit response identifies itself.
cases.oracle: No untyped 500 in the burst.

cases.title: Errors follow one shape across the module
cases.why: The whole regression guard rests on this convention: failures are `{code, message}` with a 422, so an untyped 500 is definitionally an exception.
cases.steps: Collect twenty refusals from across this file.
cases.expected: Every one carries a numeric code and a human message.
cases.oracle: No refusal without a code; report any that lack one.

cases.title: Timestamps and timezones are consistent across reads
cases.why: Buyer and vendor must agree on when bidding ends; a mixed representation is a fairness bug.
cases.steps: Read one event's window through the event-group, trade and vendor-facing endpoints.
cases.expected: The same instant everywhere, in one representation.
cases.oracle: Normalise all three to UTC and compare.

cases.title: Idempotency holds for every write in this file
cases.why: A sweep rather than a single case; retries are the norm and the cost of a duplicate differs wildly by endpoint.
cases.steps: Repeat each write endpoint's happy-path call once.
cases.expected: No duplicates of events, stages, audiences, bids or proposals.
cases.oracle: Row counts unchanged after the repeat; where a duplicate is created deliberately, document why.
